newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk Southern bids $9.1 billion for Conrail.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk Southern bids $9.1 billion for Conrail.

text.p: Norfolk Southern Corp. said Wednesday it offered to acquire railroad rival Conrail Inc. for about $9.1 billion in cash -- topping an $8.4 billion bid made last week by CSX Corp.

Norfolk Southern said it was beginning a cash tender offer for all outstanding common and Series A convertible junior preferred shares of Conrail at $100 a share, bettering CSX's bid for Conrail of $92.50 a share in cash and stock.
Conrail's stock, which did not immediately begin trading when the New York Stock Exchange opened Wednesday, jumped $13 to $97.50 when it began trading.
Norfolk Southern, however, dropped $3.50 to $91, also on the NYSE -- despite reporting 10 percent higher profits for the third quarter.

"This proposal is better on every point than the CSX/Conrail proposal announced last week," Norfolk Southern Chairman David R. Goode said in a statement announcing his company's bid for Philadelphia-based Conrail, which had been expected.
"A combined Norfolk Southern-Conrail will create a more balanced eastern rail system and will do so by increasing, rather than diminishing, competition in the industry," Goode said.

Norfolk Southern, a transportation holding company based in Norfolk, Va.,, said it already had commitments for $4 billion of the necessary financing from Merrill Lynch and JP Morgan and a letter indicating they are highly confident that the balance is available.

Norfolk Southern, which operates a 14,500-mile rail system in 20 states and one Canadian province, said it was prepared to negotiate a merger agreement on substantially the same terms and conditions as CSX's proposed transaction, except that it is offering all cash for Conrail's stock.

"Although we determined that it was appropriate, under the circumstances, to commence our cash tender offer, our strong preference would be to negotiate a merger agreement with you," Goode said in a letter to Conrail's board.

Goode also said in his letter that Norfolk Southern had filed a suit in U.S. District Court for Eastern Pennsylvania "to ensure that your (Conrail's) board fulfils its fiduciary obligations and to resolve certain other issues."
The company did not elaborate on the lawsuit.

Norfolk Southern said in a separate statement that its net income for the three months ended Sept. 30 grew to $202.3 million, or $1.61 a share, from $183.9 million, or $1.40 a share. Revenues expanded by 2 percent to $1.21 billion from $1.18 billion.

For the first nine months, Norfolk Southern said its net income rose 6 percent to $569.9 million, or $4.49 a share, from $535.8 million, or $4.07 a share. Revenues for the period also expanded by 2 percent to $3.59 billion from $3.51 billion.
